questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define party realignment in terms of durable electoral change
questions.stem: Revision session one, the back room: we read that support moved from one party to another while the old issues faded and a new pattern of voting settled in. What is this called?

options.text: Party realignment, when durable patterns of support shift between parties
Party reformation, when parties rename themselves to win new voters
options.misconception: confuses a change in voting patterns with a change of name

options.text: Turnout mobilisation, when supporters are brought out for one election
options.misconception: treats a lasting shift in support as one mobilisation

options.text: Ideological realignment, when every party adopts the same new position
options.misconception: assumes realignment means parties adopted identical positions

questions.explanation: A durable shift in which parties voters support and how they vote is party realignment. A rename or a one-off mobilisation does not change the pattern, and parties usually differ in position rather than converging.
questions.hint: Ask what changed in a way that lasted.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the effect of organisation on campaign capacity
questions.stem: Study circle, upstairs at the library: the circle read that a branch with 120 members and 40 volunteers raised 3,000, while a branch with 200 members but 10 volunteers raised 900. What does this suggest?

options.text: Money matters more than members, since the branch with more members raised less
options.misconception: reads the lower total as evidence membership is useless

options.text: Volunteers and organisation matter more than membership numbers alone
Both branches raised the same per member, since branch size explains the totals
options.misconception: ignores the volunteer numbers in the comparison

options.text: Raising money depends on a single local factor the figures do not capture
options.misconception: invents an unidentified cause instead of reading the data

questions.explanation: The branch with 40 volunteers raised three times as much as the one with 10, so capacity to mobilise rather than membership size drove the result. The volunteer counts are the visible difference between the branches.
questions.hint: Compare the two branches on volunteers, then on members.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why message framing affects reception
questions.stem: Revision notes, first floor common room: we were told that a message lands better when it is phrased in terms the audience already uses, and one case where it landed very well was praised. Why does phrasing matter so much?

answer.exemplar: Frame alignment works because audiences accept a message expressed in concepts they already use and understand, and the connection to their values is one they draw themselves. A campaign that borrows the language of a housing concern can attach its proposal to priorities the audience already holds, whereas a message in unfamiliar terms asks them to accept a new way of thinking before they accept the proposal it carries.

questions.explanation: A message phrased in the audience's own concepts invites them to make the connection themselves, which is frame alignment. Unfamiliar language asks people to accept a new way of thinking first.
questions.hint: Ask whether the audience or the campaign supplies the connection.

questions.explanation: The 210 who read only supporting items and the 90 who read only opposing items both narrowed their sources, so 300 of the 400 showed selective exposure. The 100 who read a mixture did not.
questions.hint: Add the two groups who read only one kind of source.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a chilling effect in participation data

stimulus.body: The report notes that 62 of the 100 neighbourhood activists surveyed said they had sent fewer emails to officials than they had two years earlier, and 28 said they had stopped contacting officials altogether. It also records that attendance at public meetings fell over the same period, and that two of the activists gave reasons of feeling watched and one of being ignored, while the rest gave no reason at all.

questions.stem: Revision meet, the old annexe: the report below describes participation. Which pattern does it show?

options.text: General political apathy, since all forms of participation have declined together
options.misconception: treats a targeted change in behaviour as general apathy

options.text: A backlash against the group, since activists are unhappy with the new leadership
options.misconception: invents a leadership dispute the report does not mention

options.text: A chilling effect, since contact with officials was cut back for stated reasons
A resource problem, since activists no longer have the money to send emails
options.misconception: supplies a financial cause for a change in behaviour

questions.explanation: Contact with officials was deliberately reduced and 28 activists stopped entirely, half giving reasons about how they were treated, which is a chilling effect. Apathy and resources are not what the report describes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change in participation was chosen or accidental.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effective number of parties
questions.stem: Study group, corner of the canteen: we were told that four parties are competing, but one has 40 percent and the rest split 60 percent, so the system behaves like fewer parties than the ballot shows. What is the measure called?

options.text: The minimum number of parties, the smallest number needed to fill the seats
options.misconception: confuses a count of competitors with a measure of competition

options.text: The ballot paper length, which shows how many parties voters can choose
options.misconception: treats the number of names on the ballot as the measure

options.text: The party membership total, the sum of all members across the parties
options.misconception: confuses membership size with the intensity of competition

options.text: The effective number of parties, a measure of how many parties compete equally

questions.explanation: The effective number of parties captures how many compete on comparable terms, so a large party and several small ones can count for less than the number of names on the ballot. Counts of competitors do not measure that.
questions.hint: Ask how many competitors behave as equals.

questions.learningObjective: Compare associational density between two towns
questions.stem: Evening class, art block: the class read that one town has 90 associations for 30,000 residents and another has 210 associations for the same population. What does this show?

options.misconception: ignores that the number of associations also differs

options.misconception: reads a lower number of associations as greater organisation

options.text: Association numbers say nothing about civic life without a population figure
options.misconception: demands data the comparison already supplies

questions.explanation: With equal populations of 30,000, the 210 associations give the second town a denser associational life than the 90 in the first. Equal population makes the comparison direct, and fewer groups do not mean more organisation.
questions.hint: Check the population base for each town before comparing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the advantage of insider lobbying
questions.stem: Study group, corner of the canteen: we were shown that a firm which employs three former officials has had 11 meetings with the ministry since January, and we argued it counts more than a small charity with 2 meetings. Why?

answer.exemplar: Insider lobbying carries an advantage because a firm with three former officials can approach ministries through people who already know the officials and the unwritten rules, so its requests receive more attention for each meeting. The inequality lies in access rather than in the number of meetings, because a small charity's two meetings can carry far less weight than one of the eleven obtained through personal contacts.

questions.explanation: Access through people who already know the officials is what makes the firm's meetings count for more, so the advantage lies in access per meeting rather than volume. Meeting counts alone measure nothing about influence.
questions.hint: Ask what each meeting is worth, not how many there are.

questions.hint: Work out the ballots cast in each group, then subtract.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify information asymmetry in a regulatory decision

stimulus.body: The memo notes that a company submitted a document on its own regulatory impact, that the document was accepted without the regulator requesting further evidence, and that rival firms had no visibility of the submission. It also records that two other submissions on the same regulation were made by firms that had supplied the regulator with supporting data beforehand.

questions.stem: Note to committee, Sable Wharf: the memo below concerns a regulatory submission. What does it show?

options.text: The process was unfair because the regulator had not checked the document's evidence
options.misconception: assumes no check means no scrutiny at all

options.text: Information asymmetry let one firm shape the outcome without others being able to respond
The other firms were disadvantaged because their submissions were poorly drafted
options.misconception: blames drafting quality that the memo does not mention

options.text: The regulator was biased, since it accepted the first submission it received
options.misconception: infers bias from a sequence the memo explains otherwise

questions.explanation: One firm supplied information the others never saw, and that shaped the decision without their being able to respond, which is information asymmetry. Nothing suggests the regulator skipped scrutiny.
questions.hint: Ask who knew what, and who could not respond.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how realignment occurs without a policy change
questions.stem: Evening revision, chemistry lab: we noted that a party kept winning new voters who did not like its old policy, and that the party did not change what it stood for. How can the same party win different voters?

answer.exemplar: Party realignment does not require every party to change its policy. When the issues that used to divide voters recede and new issues replace them, the old labels attach to new positions and new constituencies, so a party can attract voters who disagree with its historic platform because the issues that mattered to those voters have changed. The party is read afresh through the current issues rather than its old record.

questions.explanation: Realignment happens when the issues dividing voters change and old labels are read afresh, so a party can win voters who dislike its historic policy. Parties keep their positions while the label changes meaning.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the issues, not to the party's platform.

questions.hint: Divide the new members by the number of branches.

options.misconception: attributes the result to numbers the handout explains otherwise

options.text: The second campaign failed because it was badly run by inexperienced volunteers
options.misconception: blames the second campaign's organisation, which is not in dispute

Housing concerns simply attract more attention than economic ones
options.misconception: claims a fixed hierarchy of issues the handout does not test

questions.hint: Ask which campaign spoke in whose words.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define selective exposure
questions.stem: Side hall notes: we read that people tend to read, watch and listen to sources that confirm what they already believe, and to avoid the rest. What is this called?

options.text: Selective perception, when people misremember information that contradicts them
options.misconception: confuses the choice of sources with misremembering

options.text: Agenda control, when a small group decides what everyone else hears
options.misconception: assumes audiences are assigned their information

options.text: Political apathy, when people stop following politics altogether
options.misconception: treats choosing congenial sources as dropping out

options.text: Selective exposure, where audiences choose sources that confirm their views

questions.explanation: Selective exposure is the tendency to seek information that agrees with what one already believes and to avoid material that does not. It is a choice of sources, not misremembering, assigned information or withdrawal from politics.
questions.hint: Ask whether the audience chooses or is given its information.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a chilling effect across channels of contact
questions.stem: Revision meeting, the old gym: the notes record that emails to officials fell from 4,200 to 2,500 while postal letters rose slightly, and that 18 of 25 people who had stopped writing said they felt watched. What do the notes show?

options.text: A chilling effect on some channels of contact, with fear driving the change
A general fall in political interest, since all forms of contact declined
options.misconception: ignores the rise in postal letters and the stated reasons

options.text: A successful postal campaign, since people now prefer to write rather than email
options.misconception: treats a small rise in one channel as a strong preference

options.text: A change in official practice, since officials now answer emails less often
options.misconception: explains the fall by official behaviour the notes never mention

questions.explanation: Email contact fell sharply while letters rose slightly, and most of those who stopped gave fear as the reason, which points to a chilling effect on one channel. General indifference and official behaviour are not recorded.
questions.hint: Look at the channel that fell and the reason given.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the effective number of parties is calculated
questions.stem: Study notes, garden terrace: we worked out that a party with 60 percent of the vote means the system behaves like about one and a half parties, not four. How is that figure reached?

answer.exemplar: The effective number of parties is found by dividing one by the sum of the squared vote shares, so a 60 percent share contributes 0.36 and the remaining parties contribute the rest of the total. That gives a figure of roughly 1.6, which is the sense in which a contest that offers four names on the ballot can behave like a contest between one dominant party and a divided opposition.

questions.explanation: The effective number of parties is one divided by the sum of squared vote shares, so unequal shares give a figure well below the number of names on the ballot. That is why a dominant party makes the system behave like fewer competitors.
questions.hint: Recall that the measure uses the squares of the vote shares.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the pattern of access in a lobbying register

questions.stem: Library steps, evening class: the register below records lobbying meetings. What pattern does it show?

options.text: Meetings with former officials are more numerous, which proves they matter more
options.misconception: infers influence from the larger count of meetings

options.text: Insider advantage, since former officials and donors are well represented in access
Serving officials receive fewer meetings, so they must be less accessible
options.misconception: reads a lower meeting count as lower access for officials

options.text: Donations have no bearing on who gets to meet officials
options.misconception: denies a link the register records between donors and meetings

questions.explanation: Former officials in the private sector outnumber officials in meetings, and over half the meetings with officials involved donors, so access concentrates where insider and financial connections exist. Counts alone do not prove influence.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the trade-off made by attack messaging
questions.stem: Review hour, side hall: we read that a party that attacks the opponent on television tends to bring out its own supporters but puts off undecided voters. What does the tactic assume?

options.text: That undecided voters are more persuadable by argument than by attack
options.misconception: assumes voters weigh evidence more than affect

options.text: That most voters already agree with the party, so attacks cost nothing
options.misconception: assumes no undecided voters exist in the electorate

options.text: That attacks mobilise the base at the cost of deterring those not yet decided
That attack messaging raises turnout among all groups equally
options.misconception: assumes attacks raise turnout for every group

questions.explanation: Attacking the opponent reinforces existing supporters while discouraging those without a fixed choice, so the tactic trades a wider audience for a committed one. It does not lift turnout across all groups.

options.misconception: assumes submission counts can stand in for influence

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an information advantage shapes a decision
questions.stem: Group meeting, loading bay: we discussed why a company with in-house economists can shape a regulation that it alone paid to study. How does the information advantage work?

answer.exemplar: Information asymmetry works when one side can commission a study, submit it and have it treated as the evidence base for a decision, while other parties never see that material and cannot check or contest it. The regulator then decides on the record supplied by the interested party, and the other firms' arguments are made without sight of the document that carries the most weight.

questions.explanation: Commissioning a study and having it treated as the evidence gives one side an unseen advantage, so rivals cannot check the material that shapes the decision. A well funded study is not automatically a wrong one.
questions.hint: Ask who can see the material the decision-maker relies on.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify realignment from a change in a party's coalition

stimulus.body: The note records that between 1995 and 2015 a party that had drawn its support from manual workers gained substantially among professional voters, and that the party's policy on the main economic issue had not changed in that period. It also records that the party had lost almost all of its previous base, and that the issue which had organised voting had faded from public discussion.

questions.stem: Revision session, assembly hall: the note below describes a change in support. What does it show?

options.text: The party changed its policy to attract professional voters, which the note records
options.misconception: claims a policy change the note explicitly rules out

options.text: The party's new supporters are more numerous than the old base it lost
options.misconception: asserts a net gain in numbers the note does not state

options.text: Realignment through changed issues, since the old dividing issue faded and labels were read afresh
A temporary swing, because professional voters always vote for whoever is in office
options.misconception: generalises a party-specific pattern into a rule

questions.explanation: The party kept its policy, lost its old base and gained professional voters as the organising issue faded, which is realignment with labels read afresh. A changed policy or a temporary swing would look different.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the issues rather than to the party.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define resource mobilization
questions.stem: Study notes, rooftop terrace: we read that a movement grows through money, people and skills, and that the resources it can gather decide how far it gets. What is this called?

options.text: Political socialisation, the process of learning political values
options.misconception: confuses organisational capacity with learning

options.text: Cleavage structure, the pattern of social divisions within the electorate
options.misconception: confuses the resources a movement holds with social divisions

options.text: Selective exposure, the tendency of audiences to read congenial sources
options.misconception: confuses the gathering of resources with the choice of information

options.text: Resource mobilization, the capacity to gather money, people and skills

questions.explanation: Resource mobilization is the capacity of a group to assemble money, people and skills, which determines what it can achieve. Socialisation concerns learning values, and exposure concerns the choice of information.
questions.hint: Ask what the movement is able to gather and deploy.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret support differences caused by framing
questions.stem: Group work, carpark shelter: the shelter group recorded 300 respondents to a proposal worded in cost terms, 200 to the same proposal worded in fairness terms, and 500 to a neutral wording. What does the pattern show?

options.text: The two framings of one proposal drew sharply different support, so framing matters
The neutral wording was most popular, so framing had no effect on support
options.misconception: ignores the gap between the two framed versions

options.text: The proposal was rejected in every wording, so only 300 of 1,000 backed it
options.misconception: treats a single group's support as the whole result

options.text: Cost framing is always the strongest, since money is best argued about in money
options.misconception: generalises one comparison into a universal rule

questions.explanation: The same proposal drew 300 supporters framed as cost and 200 framed as fairness, so how it was put changed support, which is a frame effect. One comparison cannot make cost framing always stronger.
questions.hint: Compare the two framed versions of the same proposal.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how selective exposure insulates belief
questions.stem: Evening revision, maths block: we argued that an audience that reads only congenial news will keep its views even when the facts turn against them. Why?

answer.exemplar: Selective exposure insulates an audience because every source it attends confirms the belief it started with, so no counter-evidence ever reaches it. When the surrounding evidence changes, the person who has heard only supporting material interprets the new facts as consistent with the old belief, and confidence in that belief rises rather than falling as the facts become harder to reconcile.

questions.explanation: An audience reading only congenial material never meets the counter-evidence that would force revision, so confidence grows as facts shift. Selective exposure is about which sources are attended, not refusal to update.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience never encounters.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the increase in chilled respondents
questions.stem: Session notes, gazebo: a survey of 1,000 respondents found 300 said they had avoided contacting officials because they feared consequences, and the same survey two years earlier had found 120 who said so. How many more respondents are avoiding contact now?
questions.explanation: The 300 who now avoid contact against the 120 recorded two years earlier is an increase of 180 respondents. The rise in the number reporting fear is what the survey measures directly.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier count of fearful respondents from the later one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the effective number of parties for unequal shares

stimulus.body: The paper gives vote shares of 45 percent, 22 percent, 13 percent, 9 percent and 11 percent for five parties, and notes that the smallest of these is a regional party confined to one area. The paper states that the effective number of parties is obtained by dividing one by the sum of the squared vote shares.

questions.stem: Study group, music room: the paper below gives the vote shares. What does it show about the number of parties competing?

options.text: Five parties compete on equal terms, because five names appear on the ballot
options.misconception: counts the names on the ballot as equals in competition

options.text: Fewer than five parties compete effectively, since the shares are very unequal
The regional party is irrelevant to the calculation, since it cannot contest nationally
options.misconception: excludes a party on grounds the measure does not use

options.text: The largest party faces effective competition, because no other party reaches 45
options.misconception: treats one dominant share as a sign of competition

questions.explanation: The shares of 45, 22, 13, 9 and 11 percent are unequal, so their squared sum gives a figure well below five, which is the point of the measure. Every party counts, including the regional one.
questions.hint: Remember that the measure squares the shares before summing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define associational density
questions.stem: Revision hour, boiler room: we read that a town's character depends on how many voluntary groups it has per head of population, not simply on how many members they have. What is that figure?

options.text: The membership density, the number of members per head of population
options.misconception: confuses group numbers with the members they contain

options.text: The campaign density, the number of campaigns begun per head of population
options.misconception: focuses on one activity rather than the number of groups

options.text: Associational density, the number of voluntary groups per head of population
The organisational density, the number of paid officials per head of population
options.misconception: swaps voluntary groups for salaried officials

questions.explanation: Associational density counts voluntary groups relative to population, so it measures how densely the town's social life is organised. Membership totals, campaign counts and salaried officials are different quantities.
questions.hint: Ask what is being counted per head of population.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Relate donor status to access to officials
questions.stem: Evening class, dining hall: the hall counted 260 meetings with officials, of which 180 were with former officials now in private industry and 80 with serving officials, and 135 of the 180 meetings with former officials involved firms that had made donations. What does this show?

options.text: Former officials are more influential than serving officials, since they were met more often
options.misconception: infers influence from a count of meetings

options.text: Serving officials avoid former lobbyists, so access depends on current status
options.misconception: invents a preference the figures do not show

options.text: Donations have no relation to access, since only half the meetings involved donors
options.misconception: treats a majority share as a small minority

options.text: Access is closely linked to donor status, since 135 of 180 such meetings involved donors

questions.explanation: Of the 180 meetings with former officials, 135 involved donor firms, so access through the revolving door tracks donor status closely, which is what gives insider lobbying its weight. Meeting counts alone show no influence.
questions.hint: Compare the donor meetings with the total in that group.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the opposing turnout effects of attack messaging
questions.stem: Group notes, archive room: we discussed a party that used harsh attack advertising, and we noted that its own voters turned out in greater numbers while younger voters turned out less. What is the trade-off?

answer.exemplar: Attack messaging concentrates participation among those already committed and discourages those with no firm allegiance, because its content appeals to partisan feeling while offering the undecided nothing to approve. A party can therefore raise its own turnout above what a positive campaign would achieve and lose ground among first-time and soft voters at the same time, so the aggregate figure conceals two movements in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: Attack messaging raises turnout among the committed and lowers it among the undecided, so the overall figure hides two opposite movements, trading breadth of participation for depth of commitment.
questions.hint: Ask which groups moved in which direction.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate lobbying contacts that yield no substantive response
questions.stem: Revision meeting, greenhouse: a lobby group made 200 contacts, officials replied to 60 of them, and only 25 of those replies gave a substantive answer while the rest were holding letters. How many contacts produced no substantive response?
questions.explanation: Only 25 of the 200 contacts produced a substantive answer, so 175 produced no substantive response, counting the 140 unanswered as well as the 35 holding replies. Counting only the holding letters would give 35.
questions.hint: Count everything except the contacts that got a substantive answer.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe realignment as a change of coalition
questions.stem: Study circle, workshop: we read that a party changed the group of people it speaks for, and that the change happened because voters' concerns had changed. What does this describe?

options.text: Party realignment, in which a party's coalition is recast around new issues
Party manifesto change, in which the policy document is rewritten
options.misconception: confuses who the party speaks for with what it promises

options.text: Electoral system reform, in which the rules for counting votes change
options.misconception: confuses a change in voters with a change in counting

options.text: Turnout increase, in which more people reach the polls than before
options.misconception: treats a change of coalition as a change of participation

questions.explanation: A party that comes to speak for a different group because the issues have changed is undergoing realignment. Rewriting a manifesto, changing the counting rules and raising turnout are separate developments.
questions.hint: Ask who the party now speaks for and why.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare resource mobilisation efficiency per member
questions.stem: Evening session, corridor bench: the bench worked out that a branch collecting 4,000 a month from 500 members raised 8 a head, while one collecting 2,400 from 200 members raised 12 a head. What does this suggest?

options.text: The larger branch is more effective, since it raises more money overall
options.misconception: confuses the larger total with the better rate

options.text: Smaller groups can be more efficient per member, so size is not the whole story
Both branches are equally effective, since their totals are close together
options.misconception: ignores the difference in membership between the two branches

options.text: The smaller branch is failing, because it raises less than the larger one
options.misconception: judges performance by the total rather than the rate

questions.explanation: The smaller branch raises 12 a head against 8, so resources can be mobilised more efficiently at a smaller scale and size alone does not explain effectiveness. Totals without a per member rate would mislead.
questions.hint: Convert both totals into a per member figure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain a campaign failure caused by a mismatched frame
questions.stem: Group work, scout hut: we were told a campaign failed because its message assumed voters shared a set of priorities that most of them did not have. What went wrong?

answer.exemplar: The campaign's problem was that its frame did not connect with the audience's own experience, so the proposal looked like a threat to things the audience valued rather than a defence of them. Frame alignment requires a message expressed in terms that resonate with the priorities people already hold, because a proposal that appears to serve an unrelated goal will not be mobilised behind, however sound the policy may be.

questions.explanation: A frame that ignores the audience's priorities makes a proposal look like a threat rather than a defence, so the message fails to connect. Sound policy cannot compensate for a frame that does not resonate.
questions.hint: Ask how the proposal appeared to the people it addressed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of selectively exposed voters
questions.stem: Revision notes, woodshed: in a panel of 500 voters, 300 read only sources favouring their own party, 100 read only sources favouring others, and 100 read both kinds. What percentage were selectively exposed?
questions.explanation: The 400 voters who read only one kind of source out of 500 are 0.80, that is 80 percent. The remaining 100 read a mixture and so were not selectively exposed on this measure.
questions.hint: Add the two narrow groups and divide by the panel size.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a chilling effect caused by public naming

stimulus.body: The report records that a local newsletter listed the names of residents who had signed a petition about a planning application, that two of the signatories later withdrew their support, and that the following month's meeting attracted no speakers on the issue. The report also notes that petitions about the same application in two neighbouring areas, which were circulated without names, attracted speakers at every meeting.

questions.stem: Evening class, gym store: the report below describes participation in one area. What does it show?

options.text: The planning application was unpopular, which is why people stopped speaking
options.misconception: reads a fall in speakers as evidence of opposition

options.text: The named petitioners were wrong about the application, so they withdrew in embarrassment
options.misconception: invents a reason for withdrawal the report does not give

options.text: Meetings in that area always attract few speakers, whatever the petition
options.misconception: assumes a local habit the comparison contradicts

options.text: A chilling effect, since naming people visibly discouraged them from taking part

questions.explanation: Signing was made visible by the names, speakers stopped coming, and the same issue elsewhere with unnamed petitions kept its speakers, so visibility chilled participation. Unpopularity is not what the report records.
questions.hint: Compare the named and unnamed petitions in the two areas.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the effective number of parties measures
questions.stem: Study group, loading bay: we read that four parties won seats last year, but that only two and a half of them really competed for the same votes. What does that phrase mean?

options.text: That two and a half parties were eligible to contest, and one was disqualified midway
options.misconception: reads the figure as a literal count of parties present

options.text: That unequal vote shares made the system behave like fewer than four competitors
That the electorate was so large that four parties were a small number
options.misconception: confuses electorate size with the number of competitors

options.text: That two parties merged during the campaign to make four in total
options.misconception: invents a merger to explain a mathematical measure

questions.explanation: The effective number of parties measures how many competitors are of comparable strength, so uneven vote shares give a figure below the number of parties that won seats. It is a property of the vote distribution.
questions.hint: Ask how comparable the parties' support actually was.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret density against the number of active groups
questions.stem: Revision hour, back stair: the group compared two suburbs of equal population, 30,000 each, with 60 associations in one and 240 in the other, and noted that only 40 of the 240 had members at all. What does this show?

options.text: The second suburb has more association bodies, but far fewer with actual members
The first suburb is more densely organised, because its groups are genuine
options.misconception: judges density by group quality rather than group numbers

options.text: The second suburb has twice the density, since it has four times the associations
options.misconception: misreads the ratio of the two association counts

options.text: Neither suburb is more organised, since density cannot be measured without income data
options.misconception: demands data the comparison does not require

questions.explanation: With equal populations, 240 associations against 60 is a real difference in the number of bodies, but only 40 of the 240 have members, so many are dormant. Density needs no income data.
questions.hint: Compare the counts and then check how many groups are active.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain unequal access as a feature of lobbying
questions.stem: Session notes, gatehouse: we read that a small business spent less on lobbying than a large one but obtained a favourable meeting earlier, and the business blamed the fact that its trade body was unknown to officials. What is at work?

answer.exemplar: Unequal access is the issue, because a large organisation can afford to maintain staff, former officials and a network of contacts that a small business cannot, so its requests reach the decision-maker with weight attached. The smaller firm is not making a weaker case; it is arriving without the standing, the preparation or the personal access that make a case persuasive, which is what makes lobbying an unequal contest.

questions.explanation: The larger organisation can afford staff, former officials and contacts, so its request arrives with weight attached, which is unequal access rather than a weaker case. Access and familiarity are the currency here.
questions.hint: Ask what the small business lacked other than money.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how published data creates asymmetry in consultation

stimulus.body: The dossier states that a regulator received 60 submissions on a draft rule, that 41 of them came from one large association, and that the association's submission included a cost analysis that no other submitter saw. It also records that the regulator published the association's figures in the consultation document without asking other submitters for comparable data, and that the final rule followed the figures in the consultation document.

questions.stem: Evening revision, cloakroom: the dossier below concerns a consultation. What does it show?

options.text: The association was consulted more often than the other submitters, which is unfair
options.misconception: confuses one detailed submission with repeated consultation

options.text: Information asymmetry shaped the outcome, since the published figures came from one submitter
The regulator acted reasonably, because publishing data is always in the public interest
options.misconception: treats publication of one party's data as neutrality

options.text: The final rule reflected the association's figures, which proves the association won
options.misconception: treats consistency with a submission as a win for the submitter

questions.explanation: The consultation published one submitter's figures and the final rule followed them, so the other 59 submitters argued without sight of the material that carried most weight. Publication alone is not neutrality.
questions.hint: Ask which figures ended up in the document people read.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a party's rise under changed issue conditions
questions.stem: Study circle, drying room: the circle read that a party moved from 22 percent of the vote to 39 percent as the main economic issue lost salience, and that the party's policy had not changed. What does this show?

options.text: The party won more votes because it changed policy, which the figures must reflect
options.misconception: asserts a policy change the figures contradict

options.text: The party simply turned out more of its existing supporters, with no new voters
options.misconception: assumes turnout effects without any turnout data

options.text: Support shifted to the party as the old issue faded, which is a realignment pattern
The party's rise was temporary, since no issue now organises voting for it
options.misconception: assumes temporary changes must accompany any shift

questions.explanation: Support rose by 17 points as the organising issue lost salience while the party's policy stood still, which is the pattern of realignment with the party re-read through new conditions. A turnout effect would need turnout data.
questions.hint: Ask what changed: the party, the issues or the turnout.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why membership size does not equal capacity
questions.stem: Revision notes, hayloft: we read that a union branch with more members could not mount a campaign because it had no organisers, no money and no legal advisers. How should we read that?

answer.exemplar: The branch's difficulty shows that size of membership is not capacity. Resource mobilization refers to the money, paid organisers, legal advice and skill that a movement can command, and a branch without them cannot convert its members into action no matter how many it has. This is why organisational investment is treated as a separate variable from the size of the following.

questions.explanation: Members without organisers, money or legal advice cannot be converted into action, so capacity depends on resources rather than headcount. Membership size and organisational capacity are distinct variables.
questions.hint: Ask what turned members into participants.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share endorsing a matching frame

questions.explanation: The 240 respondents who endorsed the matching frame out of 600 surveyed is 0.40, that is 40 percent. The 180 who saw a neutral frame are not counted in either the matching or the conflicting group.
questions.hint: Divide the matching group by the total surveyed.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret patterns of source use

stimulus.body: The survey asked 1,200 people which sources they had used in the previous month, and 380 of them reported using only sources that supported their own party, 90 only sources that opposed it, 40 only neutral sources, and 690 a mix of two or more kinds. options.misconception: ignores what the mixed group actually included

options.misconception: reads a leading group as negligible

options.text: Selective exposure is common but not universal, and mixing sources aids recall of counter-arguments

questions.explanation: Selective use accounts for 510 of 1,200 people, substantial but leaving a large mixed group, and that group recalled counter-arguments better, so mixing counters selectivity. Source choice relates to partisanship without being universal.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define a chilling effect
questions.stem: Study group, printing works: we read that even where nothing illegal was done, people stopped taking part because they believed being seen would cost them. What is that called?

options.text: A chilling effect, where the risk of being seen discourages participation
A boycott of participation, where a group agrees to stop attending
options.misconception: treats a fear-driven retreat as an organised refusal

options.text: Selective exposure, where people avoid news that could trouble them
options.misconception: confuses avoiding participation with avoiding information

options.text: The chilling effect of a media audience, where a small audience dislikes a programme
options.misconception: reads the phrase as referring to television ratings

questions.explanation: A chilling effect is the discouragement of participation through the perceived risk of visibility, and no illegality is required for it to operate. A planned refusal, avoiding information and small audiences are different things.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the effective number of parties for three-way competition
questions.stem: Revision hour, ticket office: the ticket office noted vote shares of 55, 25 and 20 percent for three parties and computed the effective number of parties as about 2. What does this show?

options.text: Three parties compete, so the effective number must be three
options.misconception: assumes the measure must equal the count of competitors

options.text: The dominant party is small, since it holds only 55 percent of the vote
options.misconception: reads a bare majority as a small share

options.text: The opposition is unified, because the two smaller parties together hold 45 percent
options.misconception: merges two competitors into one bloc for the calculation

options.text: The system behaves like about two competitors, since the third party is small

questions.explanation: Squaring and summing 0.55, 0.25 and 0.20 gives 0.465, and one divided by that is about 2.15, close to the figure noted. The measure counts comparable competitors, and the two opposition parties are not merged.
questions.hint: Remember the sum of the squared shares, not the count of parties.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess low associational density as a precondition for civic decline
questions.stem: Notes, signal box: we read that a town's voluntary groups collapsed and civic activity fell, and that the town's density of associations had been low compared with others. How should this be read?

answer.exemplar: Low associational density is a plausible precondition for the collapse, because a town with few voluntary groups has few places for people to meet, organise and develop the capacity to resist decline. Density on its own does not cause civic weakness, since many dense towns also suffer, but it limits the stock of organisations through which collective action could have been mounted when the shock arrived.

questions.explanation: A low density leaves few organisations through which collective action could have been organised, making it a plausible precondition for collapse. Density is not a cause on its own, and many dense towns also decline.
questions.hint: Ask what the town's groups would have been able to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the differential turnout effect of attack messaging

stimulus.body: The trial recorded that two comparable districts received different campaigns before a by-election, one using repeated attack messages against the opponent and the other using positive messages about its own candidate. The report says turnout in the attacked district's polling stations was 2 percentage points lower than in the positive district, and that first-time voters fell by 4 points while habitual voters rose slightly.

questions.stem: Evening session, weighbridge: the trial below compares two campaigns. What does it show?

options.text: Attack messages raised turnout, since the attacked district polled more votes
options.misconception: reads a turnout change as a vote change

options.text: Habitual voters are the group most swayed away by attack advertising
options.misconception: reverses which group the report says fell

options.text: Attack messaging lowered turnout, and the loss fell on first-time voters
The two districts were so different that the comparison proves nothing
options.misconception: dismisses a designed comparison the report describes

questions.explanation: Turnout was lower in the attacked district and the decline was concentrated in first-time voters, while habitual voters rose, which points to attack messaging deterring the less committed.
questions.hint: Look at which group's turnout fell in each district.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define information asymmetry in a lobbying exchange
questions.stem: Study circle, pumphouse: we read that a lobbying document gets more weight when the officials have not seen anything counterbalancing it, and that the interests behind such a document are rarely visible. Which idea is that?

options.text: Selective exposure, since officials choose what to read and leave the rest
options.misconception: treats officials' reading habits as the cause of the advantage

options.text: Frame alignment, since the document is written in persuasive terms
options.misconception: confuses a document's wording with the information behind it

options.text: Effective lobbying, since the document achieved its purpose with the officials
options.misconception: treats success as evidence about the structure of the contest

options.text: Information asymmetry, where one side's material reaches the decision-maker unseen

questions.explanation: An advantage that comes from the other side never seeing the material is information asymmetry, and the interests behind it can stay hidden. Wording and success are separate from the structure of the information.
questions.hint: Ask who has not seen the material the decision rests on.
